Urmila had chosen the venue for the college fest talk: the open-air court by the canteen. Everyone nodded. Dhruv thought it was a bold idea, and he wanted the fest to go well. But he had seen dark clouds all week. He put his hand up. “Urmila, I'm with you on the open-air court, and I'll set it all up. But if it rains on Saturday we have no backup, and two hundred people will be standing in it. Can we book the seminar hall as plan B?”

Urmila paused. “Book it.”

Dhruv sent the request that afternoon. On Saturday it rained at noon, and the seminar hall was ready. Urmila only said, “Thanks for saying it.”

qa.q: Where had Urmila chosen to hold the fest talk?
qa.a: Urmila had chosen the open-air court by the canteen.

qa.q: What was Dhruv thinking when he put his hand up?
qa.a: Dhruv liked the bold idea and wanted the fest to succeed, but worried because of the dark clouds and the lack of a backup.

qa.q: What choice did Dhruv make that helped the fest?
qa.a: Dhruv backed the open-air plan but plainly asked for the seminar hall as plan B, and booked it that afternoon.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt when Dhruv raised the risk in front of everyone?
qa.a: Urmila may have felt a flash of defensiveness at a plan being questioned, but was willing to listen since Dhruv backed the direction.

grounding: A team member supports the group's direction but says plainly when a problem is visible, showing loyalty and honesty together.

“So the plan is, we finish the entire prototype by Wednesday,” Payal said, looking around the lab table.

“I'm in,” said Kashish. “I'll take the casing. But Payal, one thing. The battery we ordered won't fit the casing. I checked twice.”

“It fits in the drawing.”

“The drawing has the old measurements. If we go ahead, we'll waste two days.”

Nikhil grimaced. “Or we just make the casing bigger.”

“Yes,” Payal said, half laughing, half sighing. “Fine. Kashish, thanks for saying it now and not on Wednesday.”

“I want it to work,” said Kashish. “I'm with you all the way to Wednesday.”

Payal pulled the drawing across the table and started crossing out the old numbers.

qa.q: By when did Payal want the prototype finished?
qa.a: Payal wanted the entire prototype finished by Wednesday.

qa.q: What did Kashish want when raising the battery problem?
qa.a: Kashish was worried the prototype would fail and wanted to save the two days that going ahead with old measurements would waste, while staying with the plan.

qa.q: What choice did Kashish make that Payal was thankful for?
qa.a: Kashish agreed to the plan but plainly said the battery would not fit, and said it before Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt when Kashish challenged the drawing?
qa.a: Payal was probably irritated for a moment, but relieved to learn of the problem early, as the half-laughing sigh suggests.

grounding: A team member supports the group's direction but says plainly when a problem is visible, showing loyalty and honesty together.

passage:
I'm Thomas, and on the college trek last year, I learned what a good team member does.
Jagdish was our trek leader. He'd planned the route for weeks, and I believed in it. It was a great route. But on the second morning, I checked our water. Half the bottles were empty, and his map showed no stream for eight hours.
I didn't want to undermine him in front of everyone. So I walked beside him and said, “I'm with you on the route. But we're short on water. Can we take the lower path past the village?”
Jagdish frowned, then looked at the bottles. “Good catch.” We took the lower path, refilled at the village tap, and finished the route that evening.

qa.q: How many hours did the map show with no stream?
qa.a: Eight hours.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel before speaking to Jagdish?
qa.a: Thomas felt loyal to the plan but worried about the water, and careful not to undermine the leader.

qa.q: What made Thomas's way of raising the problem valuable?
qa.a: Thomas showed support for the route, stated the problem plainly and offered a solution privately, so the leader could adjust without losing face.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have felt when he said "Good catch"?
qa.a: He was probably a bit surprised but grateful to have a team member who told him the truth.

grounding: A student recalls supporting a trek leader's plan while plainly naming a water problem, showing loyal and honest followership.

passage:
Research supervisor's note, final-year project group, Week 7.
Ira leads the group studying street vendors' income. Her plan is strong, and the group supports her. Today Jeevan, in the planning meeting, said: “I'm fully with Ira's plan, and I'll do my share of the surveys. But I think we're only surveying on weekdays. Weekend vendors are a different group. We might miss half the picture.”
The room went quiet. Ira looked surprised, then thoughtful. She said, “You're right. Can you draft a weekend schedule?”
I was pleased. Jeevan didn't undermine Ira, and he didn't stay silent. I will mention this approach in next week's class on teamwork, without naming anyone.

qa.q: Which days was the group only surveying?
qa.a: Only on weekdays.

qa.q: How did Ira seem to feel when Jeevan raised the issue?
qa.a: She looked surprised at first, then thoughtful and open, agreeing he was right.

qa.q: Why was Jeevan's contribution a model of good followership?
qa.a: He clearly supported the plan and the leader, and still named the problem plainly with a reason, so the group improved.

qa.q: How might the other group members have felt in that quiet moment?
qa.a: They may have felt tense at first, unsure how Ira would react, then relieved that it helped.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a student who supports the leader's plan yet plainly names a problem, combining loyalty and honesty.

passage:
Wednesday
Our startup club pitch is on Friday. Lalremsiami is our team lead, and I really believe in her idea, a delivery service for village farmers. I'd follow her anywhere.
But today, going through the numbers, I saw that our fuel costs were way too low. If the judges check, the whole plan falls apart.
At the meeting, I said, “Siami, I'm all in on this. And I think the fuel numbers are too low. Can I fix them tonight?” For a second, nobody spoke. Then she said, “Oh no. Yes, please.”
I stayed up till one fixing them. I'm tired but happy. I didn't want to be the guy who stayed quiet just to be nice.
Imran

qa.q: What were too low in the plan?
qa.a: The fuel costs.

qa.q: How does Imran feel after staying up to fix the numbers?
qa.a: Imran feels tired but happy, glad about speaking up rather than staying quiet.

qa.q: What made Imran's way of speaking up effective?
qa.a: Imran showed full support, named the problem plainly and offered to fix it, so the leader could accept help without feeling challenged.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt when Imran raised the problem?
qa.a: She seemed briefly worried, then grateful, saying yes to his offer to fix it.

grounding: A student writes about backing the team lead's idea while plainly naming a flaw in the numbers, showing loyal and honest followership.
